place: Horse Creek mouth on North Platte River, near WY-NE line; territory between North Platte and Arkansas rivers
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), Sept. 17, 1851
instrument_cite: Kappler II:594-595 (as cited by PSL); atlas cites 11 Stat. 749
summary: The 1851 treaty recognized a Cheyenne and Arapaho territory bounded by the North Platte, the Rocky Mountain main range, the Arkansas to the Santa Fe road crossing, and a line to the Platte forks. Tribes kept hunting, fishing and passage rights over other tracts and did not abandon claims to other lands.
verbatim_quote: The territory of the Cheyennes and Arrapahoes [sic], commencing at the Red Bute [sic], or the place where the road leaves the north fork of the Platte River; thence up the north fork of the Platte River to its source
federal_account_contrast: Royce/atlas treat this as 'described_or_recognized' territory then ceded 1861; PSL stresses it was recognized national territory, not public domain.
map_implication: Draw Royce 426 as 1851 promised/recognized Cheyenne-Arapaho territory (with Art. 5 reservation of rights to other lands) before showing any cession layer.
notes: Boundary text quoted in full on pp.171-172; adequate to map. Note Art. 5 proviso: nations 'do not hereby abandon or prejudice any rights or claims they may have to other lands'.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), Sept. 17, 1851
instrument_cite: Kappler II:594-595 (as cited by PSL); atlas cites 11 Stat. 749
summary: The Senate in 1852 cut annuities from 50 years to 10 (plus 5 at the President's discretion). PSL says the treaty is not in the NARA registered treaties catalog 'evidently because it was never legally ratified', yet courts and squatters later relied on it.
verbatim_quote: The Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851 (Horse Creek Treaty) is not included in the U.S. Archives catalog of registered treaties, evidently because it was never legally ratified.
sources_cited_by_source: Kappler 1904:595 (endnote 18); no cite for ratification status
federal_account_contrast: Atlas cites 11 Stat. 749 as if a ratified treaty; Royce Schedule itself notes 'never ratified'. Ratification status is contested.
map_implication: Mark 1851 Fort Laramie as 'Senate-amended; ratification status contested' rather than plain ratified; show annuity term reduced 50->10 yrs.
notes: PSL does not say whether the Arapaho assented to the Senate amendment. Status needs checking against NARA and Kappler footnote.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), Sept. 17, 1851 Art. 6 (head chiefs)
instrument_cite: Kappler II:594-595 (as cited by PSL); atlas cites 11 Stat. 749
summary: Article 6 required each nation to name a head chief, an office Arapaho governance did not have. Arapahos named Little Owl as head chief; Little Owl, Big Man (Northern) and Cut Nose (Southern) signed.
verbatim_quote: The Arapaho system of governance did not have a “head chief.”
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents signers as national authorities; PSL frames the head-chief role as an imposed fiction conditional on US support and annuities.
map_implication: In signer metadata for 1851, note that 'head chief' was a US-imposed role; list Arapaho signers Little Owl, Big Man, Cut Nose.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), Sept. 17, 1851 Arts. 2-3
instrument_cite: Kappler II:594-595 (as cited by PSL); atlas cites 11 Stat. 749
summary: To Arapahos and Cheyennes the spoken council after the pipe was the real treaty, and they understood it to bind US troops to protect them from migrants. The US enforced only the written text.
verbatim_quote: To Arapahos and Cheyennes, speeches of the council after a smoke were viewed as the actual ‘treaty,’ and White Antelope later insisted that the treaty obligated troops to protect, not attack, Natives.
federal_account_contrast: Kappler text is only the written terms; Native understanding of protection obligations is absent from the federal record.
map_implication: Add an 'Indigenous understanding' note to the 1851 treaty record: protection duty under Art. 3 was central.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), Sept. 17, 1851 Arts. 4, 7, 8
instrument_cite: Kappler II:594-595 (as cited by PSL); atlas cites 11 Stat. 749
summary: Article 4 made tribes liable for 'depredations' while Article 8 let the President withhold annuities; there was no mechanism for tribes to enforce US violations, and promised protection never came.
verbatim_quote: Nowhere in the treaty is there provision for the tribes to enforce violations by the U.S. or its citizens.
federal_account_contrast: Adds structural asymmetry not shown in federal framing.
map_implication: Note one-sided enforcement in treaty summary.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), Sept. 17, 1851
instrument_cite: Kappler II:594-595 (as cited by PSL); atlas cites 11 Stat. 749
summary: PSL lists the Shoshone as attending the 1851 council though not invited.
verbatim_quote: Shoshone (attended though not invited)
federal_account_contrast: Federal party list omits uninvited attendees.
map_implication: Note Shoshone presence (not a party) at Fort Laramie 1851.

place: Plains between North Platte and Arkansas rivers; 'Arapahoe County', Kansas Territory
instrument: Kansas-Nebraska Act 1854; Kansas territorial act creating Arapahoe County 1855
summary: Kansas Territory's legislature declared the Arapaho-Cheyenne treaty land 'Arapahoe County' open to settlement in 1855, though the Kansas-Nebraska Act excluded Indian lands from the territory until the tribe assented.
verbatim_quote: all Indian lands “shall be excepted out of the boundaries, and constitute no part of the Territory of Kansas until said tribe shall signify their assent
federal_account_contrast: Federal maps show Kansas/Colorado territorial jurisdiction over this area from 1854/1861; PSL shows it was legally excluded.
map_implication: Flag Royce 426 for 1854-1861 as Indian land excluded from Kansas Territory; show 1855 Arapahoe County as unlawful local action.

place: Confluence of Cherry Creek and South Platte (Denver, Auraria, St. Charles, Montana Town); Boulder City; Black Hawk
instrument: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act June 30, 1834; Townsite Act 1844 (misused)
summary: Pikes Peak gold rush squatters founded Denver, Auraria and other towns (1858) and Boulder City (1859) on unceded 1851 treaty land, claiming the 1844 Townsite Act, which did not apply to Indian land. About 100,000 trespassers arrived 1858-1861; none was fined or removed under the 1834 Act.
verbatim_quote: gold-crazy squatters, claiming to be using the Federal Townsites Act of 1844—which did not apply to unceded Indian lands—established illegal towns at the confluence of Cherry Creek and the South Platte
sources_cited_by_source: no endnote for this paragraph; Unrau 1964:305-306 for legal analysis
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows no event between 1851 recognition and 1861 cession; the city-building happened entirely before any cession.
map_implication: Add a 1858-1861 'trespass before cession' layer on Royce 426 with Denver (39.75,-105.00) and Boulder; label towns as founded on unceded treaty land.
notes: Black Hawk named as site of discovery that set off the rush (1858); historically the 1859 Gregory Gulch strike; PSL dating may be loose.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861 Art. 11 (struck by Senate)
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: Article 11 of Fort Wise would have had the tribes sell the Denver townsite to its occupants at a minimum $1.25/acre. The Senate struck it. PSL and Unrau read it as an admission that Denver sat on Indian land and that the cession clauses did not clearly cover the upper South Platte.
verbatim_quote: this attempt to circumvent the public domain laws constituted further proof that the cession clauses of the Fort Wise agreement were of little value as a means of nullifying tribal claims to the upper South Platte basin
federal_account_contrast: Royce/Kappler show Fort Wise as a clean cession; the struck Article 11 shows the US knew Denver title was defective.
map_implication: Attach a note to Denver area: Senate-struck Art. 11 (Fort Wise) acknowledged Indian title; never paid.

place: Fort Wise (later Fort Lyon), Arkansas River
instrument: Greenwood council preceding Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: Commissioner Greenwood stayed 12 days, met only a few Southern leaders (Black Kettle, White Antelope, Little Raven, Left Hand), who refused his treaty. He reported success anyway. Northern Arapahos and Cheyennes were absent.
verbatim_quote: Only a few tribal leaders with questionable authority made verbal promises to exchange their princely domain for government annuities
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents Fort Wise as agreement with the tribes; scholarship shows no real negotiation and no northern participation.
map_implication: Flag Royce 426 cession: Northern Arapaho and Northern Cheyenne not present at any stage.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: Agent A.G. Boone gathered a few hungry Southern leaders in winter and presented Greenwood's text without negotiation. Arapaho marks: Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head, Big Mouth. No Northern Arapahos; Left Hand absent and not contacted. Signers said they spoke only for their own bands.
verbatim_quote: No Northern Arapahos were present. Important Southern Arapahos, especially Left Hand, were not present.
federal_account_contrast: Royce credits the cession to 'Arapaho and Cheyenne of the Upper Arkansas' as a whole.
map_implication: Flag Royce 426 as 'signed by four Southern Arapaho band leaders only; no Northern Arapaho signers'.
notes: Tension: p.177 says Little Raven left the Sept 1860 meeting and p.184 says he repudiated the treaty, yet p.182 lists him as a signer.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: PSL says the Arapahos were suffering severe hunger and that provisions were commonly used to induce signatures; tribal descendants state the US threatened starvation unless leaders accepted the barren reserve.
verbatim_quote: At negotiations over the 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise, the US government threatened us with starvation unless our leaders agreed to stay on a tiny piece of barren land
sources_cited_by_source: History Colorado Sand Creek Massacre exhibition 2022-2023 (endnote 64), text by Cheyenne and Arapaho descendants
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows no duress.
map_implication: Flag Royce 426 cession as signed under starvation duress (Indigenous account).
notes: Descendant statement is exhibit text; PSL's own narrative is less explicit ('Most certainly the Arapahos were suffering severe hunger').

place: Fort Wise; Huerfano River mouth; Sulphur Spring on Arkansas
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861 and P.S.
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: Boone was building a ranch on usurped Indian land at the Huerfano mouth that the treaty would legitimize. Interpreters Robert Bent and John S. Smith, who PSL says spoke no Arapaho, received 640-acre grants for themselves/kin via a treaty postscript.
verbatim_quote: At the time he was building a ranch at the mouth of the Huerfano River, on a section of Indian land he had already usurped.
federal_account_contrast: Not in federal framing.
map_implication: Note interpreter and agent self-dealing in Fort Wise record; map the two 640-acre P.S. grants if locatable.
notes: The P.S. grants are to Robert Bent and to Jack Smith (son of John S. Smith).

place: Sand Creek Reservation: Arkansas River from Sandy Fork to Purgatoire, south to NM line
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861 Arts. 1-6
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: Fort Wise reserved a tract from the mouth of Sandy Fork west along the Arkansas to the Purgatoire, up the Purgatoire to New Mexico's north line, west to a line due south of a point 5 miles east of the Huerfano mouth, then north to beginning. Eastern part to the Arapaho. It was dry, far from bison; promised houses, mill and tools never came, and agent Colley leased part to whites.
verbatim_quote: Beginning at the mouth of the Sandy Fork of the Arkansas River and extending westwardly along the said river to the mouth of Purgatory River
federal_account_contrast: Royce 477 shows reserve then 1865 cession; PSL adds that it was never delivered as promised and was leased to whites.
map_implication: Draw Royce 477 as promised reserve that was never furnished; note Colley leasing (c. late 1863/1864).
notes: PSL says the then New Mexico line ran just south of the Arkansas.

place: Upper South Platte basin north and west of South Platte
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861 Art. 6
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: Article 6 barred non-signers who did not rejoin within one year from the treaty's benefits. US Attorney S.E. Browne read the 1851 and 1861 treaties to mean no lawful white settlement north and west of the South Platte after Dec. 6, 1862, and Dole briefly agreed, before reversing under pressure.
verbatim_quote: Browne saw no legality for white settlement north and west of the South Platte.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows all of 426 ceded in 1861; a contemporary federal attorney concluded otherwise.
map_implication: Show the area north/west of the South Platte (incl. Denver north side, Golden, Boulder, mining districts) as 'contested: not ceded by Fort Wise per 1862 US Attorney reading'.
notes: Browne's view also implied land south of the South Platte was ceded, which non-treaty bands rejected (p.185).

instrument: Dole letter reversing Browne; Evans authority
summary: Under pressure from Evans and settlers, Commissioner Dole reversed himself in a 'wordy, ambiguous' letter claiming Fort Wise ceded all lands; the US chose defiance of federal law as a fait accompli.
verbatim_quote: defiance of federal law and recognition of the whole affair as a fait accompli
federal_account_contrast: Shows cession validated by administrative fiat, not consent.
map_implication: Add a note on Royce 426 cession: validity asserted by 1862-63 Dole letter, not by tribal assent.

instrument: Proposed Northern Arapaho reserve; Evans order to Maj. Loree
summary: Evans got Dole's permission to negotiate a reserve for Northern Arapahos on the Cache la Poudre; Little Owl, Medicine Man and Friday were willing but nothing came of it. Evans later ordered Northern Arapaho chiefs to sign assent to Fort Wise before receiving food.
verbatim_quote: He commanded a Major Loree to have Northern Arapaho chiefs sign a document stating that they agreed with Fort Wise before receiving food.
federal_account_contrast: No Northern Arapaho land base in Colorado appears in federal maps; a reserve was discussed and abandoned.
map_implication: Note a never-created Northern Arapaho reserve on the Cache la Poudre (Fort Collins area); flag any Northern Arapaho Fort Wise assent as food-conditioned.
notes: Whether Northern chiefs signed is not stated. No boundaries given.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861 annuities
instrument_cite: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
summary: Agent Samuel G. Colley, Commissioner Dole's cousin, stole Arapaho annuities and sold them back; Little Raven and Left Hand reported this without result. Colley said he had nothing for Left Hand's band though Evans had sent $3,000.
verbatim_quote: Colley continued to steal the Arapahos’ annuities, then sell them back to them.
federal_account_contrast: Not in federal treaty record.
map_implication: Attach annuity-theft note to Fort Wise and Upper Arkansas Agency.
notes: Unrau frames it as accusation and implausible denial.

instrument: Evans proclamations June 27 and Aug. 11, 1864
summary: Governor and Indian Superintendent Evans first ordered 'friendly' Indians to forts, then authorized citizens to kill 'hostile' Indians and keep their property. PSL ties the Northern Arapaho removal recommendation to these proclamations.
verbatim_quote: to kill and destroy, as enemies of the country, wherever they may be found, all such hostile Indians
federal_account_contrast: Territorial (state predecessor) action; not a treaty event.
map_implication: Add Evans proclamations as state-action events affecting all of Royce 426.

instrument: Camp Weld council
summary: At Camp Weld Evans refused to make peace with Arapaho and Cheyenne leaders and later wrote that his talk offered them nothing; Chivington's assurance that those surrendering to Wynkoop were not hostile 'turned out to be a lie'.
verbatim_quote: This turned out to be a lie, but the seven chiefs left with the impression that they would be protected
map_implication: Mark Camp Weld (Denver) as a failed peace council preceding Sand Creek.

summary: The chapter calls Sand Creek a vicious episode in a campaign of genocide and records that Left Hand (Niwot) and many of his band were killed by Chivington's force. It gives little detail of the massacre itself.
verbatim_quote: Left Hand (Niwot) had been killed by Chivington’s mob in 1864, along with many of his band.
map_implication: Mark Sand Creek inside/adjacent to Royce 477 reserve; note Arapaho dead incl. Left Hand.
notes: Date and location not given in this chapter; date from general record. Other PSL chapters may hold detail.

instrument: Act 'for the relief of the citizens of Denver' (May 1864); general townsite relief act May 23, 1864
summary: Congress in May 1864 'legalized' the 1858 Denver lots, and by 1872 the Supreme Court treated Denver as laid out 'on the public domain'. This was months before Sand Creek and the 1865 Little Arkansas cession.
verbatim_quote: was originally laid out by a company or association of persons on the public domain of the United States before the same had been surveyed
federal_account_contrast: Courts recast unceded treaty land as public domain retroactively.
map_implication: Add 1864 Denver relief act as a legal-taking event; contrast with Art. 11 struck 1861.
notes: PSL gives the date as May 24, 1864 in its text but the quoted opinion says May 28, 1864; needs checking (Stat. 13).

instrument: Homestead Act 1862; Pacific Railway Act 1862
summary: Descendants say Lincoln broke promises by signing the Homestead and Pacific Railway acts, which took homelands without consent; Evans's railroads gained land grants along tracks.
verbatim_quote: These two acts unilaterally took away Cheyenne and Arapaho homelands without full agreement from either of our Tribes.
map_implication: Flag railroad grant land and homestead entries in Royce 426 as statutory taking.
notes: PSL says companies got 'ten square miles on each side ... for each mile' (likely sections, not square miles); verify.

instrument: Indian Claims Commission award, Docket 329-D (as named by source)
summary: Northern Arapaho TREC recommendations ask Colorado to support reopening the ICC settlement, calling valuations biased and the final award 'unscrupulous and dishonorable', and questioning the 'unratified' 1851 treaty and the Fort Wise taking.
verbatim_quote: The calculations to determine values were biased.
sources_cited_by_source: Tribe's own endnote 10; no further cite
federal_account_contrast: ICC payment treated by US as extinguishment; tribe disputes it.
map_implication: Tag Royce 426 with 'ICC Docket 329 (subdocket D per source): disputed by Northern Arapaho'.
notes: No award amount, date, or acreage valuation given in this chunk. Verify docket number and award.

place: Front Range to continental divide; watershed from North Platte headwaters to South Platte confluence
instrument: Northern Arapaho TREC recommendations 1-3
summary: The tribe asserts the Front Range was 'legally titled' to Arapaho, gold taken from 1858 on land 'they never signed a treaty and ceded', and inherent water rights in the North Platte-South Platte watershed were never compensated.
verbatim_quote: The Arapaho were never compensated for the gold taken from 1858 to the present on the land that they never signed a treaty and ceded.
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats this as ceded 1861; Northern Arapaho say they never ceded.
map_implication: Show Northern Arapaho position: no Northern Arapaho cession of Royce 426 (Colorado portion); map the claimed watershed area.
notes: Watershed boundary is described loosely: 'from the continental divide, from the headwaters of the North Platte River to the confluence with the South Platte River and back to the continental divide'.

instrument: Northern Arapaho TREC recommendations 4-12
summary: The tribe calls its forced removal from Colorado an act of genocide tied to Evans, and seeks compensation, restored hunting/gathering rights on public lands, return of abandoned railroad land, GOCO access, tax relief, and tuition waivers; it notes the State School Fund received 4 million acres and CSU still holds 19,000 acres of Arapaho land.
verbatim_quote: The forced removal was an act of genocide.
federal_account_contrast: Removal to Wind River is not narrated in this chapter.
map_implication: Add Northern Arapaho present-day claims as a layer; note CSU and State School Fund lands.
notes: The chapter ends in 1865 and contains no account of the move to Wind River (1878) or the 1868 Fort Laramie / Fort Bridger arrangements.

summary: Harney's 1855 campaign killed 86 Sioux and took 70 hostages and threatened Northern Arapahos who had not fought; Sumner's 1857 campaign kept Southern Arapahos from hunting, deepening starvation. Agent Whitfield said Indians must be 'whipped into submission' before new treaties.
verbatim_quote: claimed that Indians would have to be “whipped into submission” before treaties addressing the changed situation in Colorado could be negotiated
federal_account_contrast: Pre-Fort Wise coercive context missing from federal treaty record.
map_implication: Context note for Fort Wise duress.

summary: Drunken miners attacked Left Hand's village on Cherry Creek while the men were away, raping women and stealing horses; the Rocky Mountain News used it to argue for extinguishing Indian title.
verbatim_quote: the necessity of extinguishing the Indians’ title
map_implication: Note Arapaho village on Cherry Creek, Denver, 1860 as occupied Arapaho homeland.
